title: Deductible Roulette
primary_metric: expected total dollars spent on auto insurance (premium plus probability-weighted deductible exposure) over a three-year ownership window, comparing a low-deductible policy (The Guarded Lane) against a high-deductible policy (The Long Shot)

options.A: The Guarded Lane -- renew the $500-deductible policy at the higher monthly premium
options.B: The Long Shot -- switch to the $1,000-deductible policy at the lower monthly premium

sources.claim: National average annual full-coverage auto insurance premium at a $500 deductible and at a $1,000 deductible (matched comprehensive/collision deductible pairing, same driver profile, same rate table)
sources.title: Auto insurance rate analysis with Quadrant Information Services
sources.note: This exact $2,638/$2,336 pairing (a $302/yr, ~11.4% premium reduction for doubling the deductible from $500 to $1,000, matched same-day/same-profile) is reported identically across multiple independent secondary sources (moneygeek.com, aol.com finance coverage, and others), each attributing it to 'Bankrate's January 2025 rate analysis with Quadrant Information Services.' Direct WebFetch attempts on several bankrate.com insurance-deductible URLs returned generic homepage/navigation content rather than the underlying article -- likely a JS-rendered or geo-gated page the fetch tool could not resolve -- so this case relies on the search-surfaced, multiply-corroborated figure rather than an independently rendered primary page. Graded MEDIUM (not HIGH) for that reason: well-attributed and consistently repeated, but not independently verified by direct fetch of the primary page. See RESEARCH_LOG.md for the full trail, including a same-family MoneyGeek pair of pages that showed the opposite (and much smaller, likely noise-level) direction and was excluded as a contested/unreliable comparison rather than used.

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC SS4

deliverables.text: A three-year claim-probability table showing, for each year, the probability of Priya filing an at-fault collision claim: Year 1's probability (Appendix B baseline), Year 2's probability given she is still claim-free entering Year 2 versus Year 2's probability given a claim already occurred in Year 1 (Appendix C), and Year 3's probability under both of those same two conditions -- with the conditioning stated in words for every row.

A compound-probability calculation, shown step by step, of the probability that Priya remains completely claim-free through both Year 1 and Year 2, and the complementary probability that she has had at least one claim by that point -- computed from Appendix B's baseline Year 1/2 figures.

A full three-year expected-cost calculation for each policy: for every year, weight that year's expected deductible payment by the probability of entering the year claim-free (baseline rate applies) versus the probability of already having a claim on record (the elevated rate from Appendix C applies), add each policy's fixed three-year premium total from Appendix A, and show the arithmetic for every term.

A written breakdown of D3's result: state how much of the winning policy's advantage is coming from the premium difference (Appendix A) alone, versus how much is coming from the weighted claim-cost difference -- and state whether the recommendation would still hold if Appendix C's elevated repeat-claim probability were meaningfully higher than the value used.

An original visual display (a bar chart, a probability tree, or equivalent) comparing The Guarded Lane's three-year total expected cost against The Long Shot's three-year total expected cost, built from the D3 figures.

appendices.title: Baseline Collision Claim Data (clean driving record)

balance.argument_a: The Guarded Lane's case is that its $500 deductible caps Priya's worst-case single-claim exposure at half of what The Long Shot would charge her, and that cap is worth something in its own right for a driver with no cash cushion -- variance reduction, not just expected-value comparison, is a legitimate reason to prefer A even though (see 'The margin' in FACILITATOR.md) A's real three-year expected cost, computed correctly, comes out higher than B's. A's argument is strongest for a Hero who weighs the psychological and cash-flow cost of an unplanned $1,000 payment more heavily than the model's raw dollar total.
balance.argument_b: The Long Shot's case is the D3 expected-cost math itself: once Appendix B's real 4.9% baseline collision-claim frequency is properly weighted against both policies' real premiums and deductibles across the full three-year window -- including the branch where a first claim raises the probability of a second one (Appendix C) -- B's three-year expected total cost comes out lower than A's, by a real, moderate margin. This is the case's central rubric trap: a Hero who picks the lower deductible by default, on the instinct that it 'feels safer,' will be choosing the option that actually costs more in the large majority of realistic three-year outcomes, because the deductible is only ever paid if a claim happens, and Appendix B's own baseline probability of that says it usually does not.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |total_expected_cost(A) - total_expected_cost(B)| / max(total_expected_cost(A), total_expected_cost(B)), where each policy's total_expected_cost = 3-year premium total (Appendix A) + sum over 3 years of [P(claim-free entering year N) x baseline_prob x deductible + P(already had a claim entering year N) x MA1_elevated_prob x deductible]. Using Appendix B's baseline_prob = 4.9%, Appendix A's premiums/deductibles, and MA1 = 20%: A total = $7,914 + $84.42 = $7,998.42. B total = $7,008 + $168.83 = $7,176.83. margin = |7998.42 - 7176.83| / 7998.42 = 10.3%. This is within the concept brief's 8-12% target band. NOTE: unlike cases/the-deferred-repair, this margin is built almost entirely from SOURCED figures (Appendix A's premiums, Appendix B's claim frequency and severity are all real, cited numbers) -- MA1 (Appendix C's elevated repeat-claim probability) is the case's one stated Modeling Assumption, and sensitivity_model.py's +/-50% sweep found it moves this primary margin only slightly (roughly 10.2%-10.4%), i.e. the headline recommendation is genuinely robust to this assumption, not fragile to it. See modeling_assumptions[MA1].sensitivity and case.json.derived for the twist-scenario finding, where the same assumption matters much more.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Probability of a subsequent at-fault collision claim in a year, given a claim already occurred earlier in the three-year window
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes a general-population percentage for this exact claim. Peer-reviewed traffic-safety literature (crash-recurrence and crash-prone-driver-clustering studies, e.g. Louisiana DOTD crash data showing a small subgroup of at-fault-prone drivers accounting for a disproportionate share of repeat crashes; subgroup studies finding several-times-elevated risk ratios for specific populations) consistently documents that a prior at-fault crash is associated with meaningfully elevated future risk, but reports it as a relative-risk ratio for a narrow subgroup or a concentration share, not as a single general-population annual percentage. 20% (roughly 4x Appendix B's 4.9% baseline) is a deliberately moderate reading of 'meaningfully elevated,' not the high end suggested by the subgroup-specific literature.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: sensitivity_model.py's +/-50% sweep (10% to 30%) moves the case's PRIMARY three-year expected-cost margin only slightly (roughly 10.2% to 10.4%), and a binary search found no value of this assumption in [0%, 100%] flips the primary recommendation -- the headline recommendation is genuinely robust to this assumption at the primary-metric level. The SAME parameter has a much larger effect on the narrower 'what if a claim already happened in Year 1' scenario Challenge 3 (D4) asks the student to check separately: because the elevated rate applies undiluted to both remaining years once a claim has occurred, that narrower calculation DOES flip at a value well within what the case's own basis note admits is plausible. Work D4 out yourself rather than assuming the two findings must move together -- they do not.
modeling_assumptions.flips_dilemma: primary metric: no (verified robust to [0,1] by binary search). D4/twist scenario: yes, at recid_prob ~60.4% -- see case.json.derived.twist_flip_threshold.

derived.notes: Figures computed from sensitivity_model.py, not restated in case.md (facilitator-only), kept here so FACILITATOR.md's Guide Notes stay checkable against a value of record instead of drifting silently.

branch_probability_weights.note: The per-year expected-deductible-payment weight, decomposed by branch (clean vs. already-claimed), used in 'The margin' arithmetic in FACILITATOR.md.

twist_recompute_after_year1_claim.note: Recomputes the remaining Year 2 + Year 3 total cost (2 years of premium + 2 years of deductible exposure at MA1's elevated rate) for a driver who has already filed one claim in Year 1 -- the D4/Twist scenario.

flip_threshold.note: sensitivity_model.py's binary search found NO value of MA1 (repeat-claim probability) in [0%, 100%] that flips the PRIMARY three-year recommendation (evaluate()) from B to A -- even at recid_prob=100% (every driver who ever files one claim is certain to file a second), B still wins, at a reduced but real ~9.5% margin. MA1 only ever weights a fraction of the 3-year window's probability mass in the primary metric, so it structurally cannot outweigh the fixed $906/3yr premium gap between the two policies. This is a genuine robustness finding for the PRIMARY metric specifically, not for every metric this case computes -- see twist_flip_threshold below, found during Tier 2 P4 adversarial review, for the metric where MA1 DOES flip the answer.

twist_flip_threshold.note: CORRECTION (2026-09-04, Tier 2 P4 finding): unlike the primary metric above, the D4/Twist scenario (evaluate_twist() -- the remaining Years 2-3 cost for a driver who has ALREADY had a claim in Year 1) DOES flip from B to A, because in that scenario MA1 applies undiluted to both remaining years (there is no 'still clean' branch left to dilute it once a claim has already occurred). sensitivity_model.py's binary search on evaluate_twist() finds the flip at recid_prob ~= 60.4% -- about 3x the case's stated 20% value, and a value the case's own MA1 basis note does not rule out ('not the high end of what the literature's subgroup-specific ratios could suggest'). An earlier draft of this file incorrectly implied no metric in this case is sensitive to MA1; that was true only for evaluate(), not evaluate_twist(). FACILITATOR.md's Twist section is corrected to state both findings explicitly and not conflate them.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The probability that a driver who has already filed one at-fault claim files a second one is a forecast about a specific individual's future behavior, not a measurable present population fact -- no dataset can say in advance whether Priya specifically would be at elevated risk. Tier 2 P5 found this dial does NOT flip the PRIMARY three-year verdict even at a very large (+50%, i.e. 30%) flex -- and sensitivity_model.py's binary search found no flip exists anywhere in [0%, 100%] for the primary metric, since this parameter only ever weights a fraction of the 3-year window's probability mass and cannot outweigh the fixed 3-year premium gap between the two policies. Disclosed here as a genuine robustness finding for the primary metric, not a fragility, consistent with house doctrine that absent/uncertain data is a first-class state that must be stated either way.

Found during Tier 2 P4 adversarial review (2026-09-04): the SAME forecast-uncertain parameter DOES flip the narrower D4/Twist scenario (the remaining Years 2-3 cost for a driver who has already had a Year-1 claim), at recid_prob ~60.4% -- about 3x the stated 20% value, and a value the case's own MA1 basis note does not rule out as implausible. This is disclosed explicitly and separately from the primary-metric finding above because they are genuinely different results on different metrics, not the same finding restated -- see case.json.derived.twist_flip_threshold and FACILITATOR.md's Twist section, both corrected to state this rather than imply blanket robustness.
